title: Shaving the hair
hook: a baby's first hair, weighed, and its weight in silver given away

segments.voice: Yesterday, the 'aqiqah, and your line: thanks for a child. Was a meal shared, or a new baby remembered? The same seventh day holds one more custom, and it fits in the palm of a hand. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-two.

A grandson has been born. His name is al-Hasan, and his mother is Fatimah, the daughter of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. The baby can't hold anything, can't say anything, can't do a single thing for anyone. And the Prophet gives his daughter an instruction about the softest, lightest thing the baby has: the hair he was born with. Not to keep it. Not to throw it away. To weigh it. Today: why a family would weigh something that light, and what they do with the answer.
screen: `A GRANDSON, A WEEK OLD.` → `THE HAIR HE WAS BORN WITH.` → `WEIGH IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the report, in Jami' at-Tirmidhi, in paraphrase. When al-Hasan was born, the Prophet said to Fatimah: shave his head, and give the weight of his hair in silver as charity. So they weighed it, the report says, and it came to a dirham, or part of a dirham. Not a fortune. A coin, maybe less. That's the first surprise: the amount is small, and the hadith says so plainly. The point isn't the size of the gift. Something taken from the child becomes something given in the child's name. Second, the half-sentence left over from yesterday. The hadith in Bukhari said: shed blood on the child's behalf, and remove harm from him. What harm? The hadith doesn't say, and some readers take it to mean this very thing: the hair the baby was born with. And a hadith in Sunan Abu Dawud, in paraphrase, sets the seventh day in one line: the 'aqiqah sacrificed, the head shaved, the child named. Sacrifice, shaving, naming, side by side. Third, what families do now. Some still shave the baby's head on the seventh day and weigh the hair. Others estimate the weight and give its value in money. Scholars discuss the details, and families follow the school and the custom they know. Fourth, look at it from the baby's side. A baby owns nothing. Can't earn, can't give, can't even hold a coin. And yet, on day seven, there's already charity written in the baby's name. Before a child can do a single good deed, the family does one for them. The child arrives in the world as a giver.
screen: `SHAVE IT. WEIGH IT. GIVE ITS WEIGHT.` · `A DIRHAM, OR PART OF ONE.` · `SACRIFICE, SHAVING, NAMING.` · `A BABY ARRIVES AS A GIVER.`

segments.voice: The practice: give in a child's name. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one child: your own, a niece, a neighbor's new baby, or the child you once were. Say their name quietly. Now think of something small you could give in that name today. A coin in a box. A meal for someone. A donation with their name on it. It doesn't need to be large; the hadith's amount wasn't. If you pray, you can ask good for that child in your own words. If you don't, just hold their name and the gift together for a while. The bell holds the time.
Shaving the hair. On the seventh day, a baby's first hair is shaved, and its weight in silver is given away in charity. Today's word.
Your line: weight in silver. Today, give something small in a child's name, and let it be light. Tomorrow, circumcision, the way of Ibrahim. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: On or around the seventh day, some Muslim families shave the newborn's head and give the weight of the hair in silver, or its value in money, to charity, alongside the 'aqiqah and the naming.

fork.setup: you're Fatimah. your son al-Hasan is a week old, and the Prophet tells you to shave his head. what happens to the hair?

save it for his wedding day.

original.note: Arabic: shaving, as of the head.

trapdoor: what you thought: a baby's first haircut.
what it means: the first hair, shaved on the seventh day and weighed, so its weight in silver goes to charity in the child's name.
what a scholar hears: Tirmidhi's report of al-Hasan, a dirham or part of one, beside Abu Dawud's hadith joining the 'aqiqah, the shaving and the naming on the seventh day.

sources.ref: Jami' at-Tirmidhi 1519 (al-Hasan's hair weighed; its weight in silver given; a dirham or part of a dirham)
Sahih al-Bukhari 5471–5472 (shed blood for him, and remove harm from him)
Sunan Abu Dawud 2838 (every child is in pledge for his 'aqiqah, sacrificed on the seventh day, his head shaved, and he is named)

notes: Hadith numbers to confirm: Tirmidhi 1519 (hair of al-Hasan), Abu Dawud 2838 (in pledge for his 'aqiqah). Both paraphrased.
